overview:
In the spring of 1966 Mao Zedong, sidelined within his own party after the catastrophe of the Great Leap Forward, launched a campaign to purge the Chinese Communist Party of officials he judged to be steering the country back toward capitalism and bureaucratic privilege. He did it by going around the party apparatus and appealing directly to the young. Schools and universities closed; students organized themselves as Red Guards and turned on teachers, writers, officials and anyone tagged with a bad class background. Temples, libraries and family collections were ransacked in the name of destroying the "four olds." Senior figures fell in sequence — Liu Shaoqi, the head of state, died in detention in 1969; Deng Xiaoping was sent to work in a tractor factory. Millions of urban youths were later dispatched to the countryside, an entire cohort's education traded for a decade of farm labor.

By early 1967 the campaign had slipped past anyone's control. Rival mass organizations, each claiming to be the true revolutionaries, seized government buildings and fought each other with weapons taken or handed out from army arsenals. The People's Liberation Army was ordered in to "support the left," which mostly meant local commanders picking sides. The clearest case is the Wuhan incident of July 1967, when General Chen Zaidao's regional command backed the conservative Million Heroes and refused Beijing's order to switch its support to the radical Workers' Headquarters. Two envoys sent from the capital, Xie Fuzhi and Wang Li, were seized and beaten; Mao, who had been secretly in the city, was flown out. Roughly a thousand people died in the fighting and its reprisals. Chen was dismissed, but the episode frightened the leadership badly — a regional army had defied the center — and it pushed Mao to rein in the Red Guards and hand authority to the military and to revolutionary committees.

The rest of the decade was quieter only by comparison. Lin Biao, named Mao's successor in the 1969 party constitution, died in a plane crash over Mongolia in 1971 while apparently fleeing after a failed plot, an event that shredded much of the movement's remaining credibility. Radicals around Mao's wife Jiang Qing — later condemned as the Gang of Four — fought the surviving pragmatists over culture, education and succession until Mao's death in September 1976. Within a month the Gang of Four were arrested, and the Cultural Revolution was over. In 1981 the party's own resolution on party history called it a catastrophe and laid principal responsibility on Mao, while preserving his overall standing.
significance: The decade broke the machinery of Chinese politics and then determined what replaced it. A generation lost its schooling, the professional and cultural classes were gutted, and the party's claim to infallibility was damaged from inside by the party itself. The reaction against that chaos is the direct foundation of the Deng Xiaoping era: economic pragmatism, collective rather than personal rule, fixed leadership terms, and a deep official aversion to mass mobilization from below. It also left a contested memory. The "scar literature" of the late 1970s aired some of the damage, but full public reckoning has never been permitted, archives remain largely closed, and the period is handled gingerly in Chinese textbooks and public discussion — which makes the Cultural Revolution one of the twentieth century's largest events with one of its most restricted historical records.
coverage: Written from Wikipedia, Britannica, and a Sciences Po chronology of mass killings, with the Wuhan incident checked separately; the dataset itself holds only that single 1967 event, so the map shows almost none of the decade's geography — the Beijing Red Guard terror of 1966, the Guangxi and Inner Mongolia massacres, the rustication of urban youth, or the Lin Biao affair. Nationwide death estimates range from roughly 750,000 to several million and do not converge, because Chinese archives are largely closed, scholars count different things (killings, forced suicides, deaths under persecution), and much of what is known comes from county gazetteers and post-Mao rehabilitation files compiled by the same party that ran the campaign.
